record.paper_title: Magic matrices with their powers, numerical ranges and some open problems
record.original_question: Let a magic matrix of order n mean an n by n square matrix whose entries are the natural numbers 1, 2, ..., n^2 with no repeated entry, and whose row sums, column sums, main diagonal sum, and antidiagonal sum are all equal. For any such matrix, let s denote the common row, column, main diagonal, and antidiagonal sum, which is an eigenvalue. Among magic matrices of the same order, how much can the eigenvalues other than s differ? May those non-s eigenvalues have arbitrary phase, and are they always symmetric with respect to zero?

evidence.quote: square matrices (of order n) satisfying the following conditions: (m1) the entries aij of A belong to the set {1, 2, . . . , n2 }, (m2) if (i, j) 6= (k, l) then aij 6= akl , (m3) the sums in each row, each column, main diagonal and antidiagonal are equal.
From now on s will denote this number. We easily verify that s is an eigenvalue of the magic matrix and a corresponding eigenvector is x = (1, 1, . . . , 1)T .

Open problem 3. The magic matrices exhibited in Remark 1.1 and Remark 2.1 have different eigenvalues (apart from s) than matrices of the same order generated by MATLAB. How much may the eigenvalues of different magic matrices of the same order differ? May they have an arbitrary phase? Are they always symmetric with respect to zero (not counting s)?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Define a magic matrix of order $n$ to be an $n \times n$ matrix $A=(a_{ij})$ with entries from the set $\{1,2,\dots,n^2\}$ such that all entries are distinct (each integer in $\{1,2,\dots,n^2\}$ appears exactly once), and such that the sum of the entries in every row, every column, the main diagonal, and the antidiagonal are all equal to a common value $s$. Since the all-ones vector $(1,1,\dots,1)^T$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $s$, the number $s = n(n^2+1)/2$ is always an eigenvalue of $A$.

For magic matrices of a fixed order $n$, investigate the variation of the remaining eigenvalues (those different from $s$). Specifically:

(a) Quantitatively bound or describe how much the non-$s$ eigenvalues can differ between two magic matrices of the same order $n$.

(b) Determine whether the non-$s$ eigenvalues of magic matrices of order $n$ can attain arbitrary complex phase (argument), or whether their arguments are constrained to a proper subset of $[0,2\pi)$.

(c) Determine whether, for every magic matrix of order $n$, the multiset of non-$s$ eigenvalues is symmetric about $0$ in the complex plane (i.e., $\lambda$ is a non-$s$ eigenvalue with multiplicity $m$ if and only if $-\lambda$ is, with the same multiplicity), or exhibit magic matrices for which this fails.
artifact.status_search_result: A targeted web search did not return any published results that resolve the question of how much the non-$s$ eigenvalues of magic matrices of fixed order can vary, whether they can take arbitrary phase, or whether they are always symmetric about zero. No follow-up work addressing these specific questions was located, so the current status appears unverified.

status_evidence.title: Magic square eigenvalue example
status_evidence.snippet: A 5-by-5 magic square has eigenvalues 65, ±21.2768, ±13.1263, illustrating symmetric non-s eigenvalues in one example.
status_evidence.claim: Numerical examples are known but no general resolution of the open question was found.
